newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Thousands march, strike in Russia, demand back pay.
newsitem.headline: Thousands march, strike in Russia, demand back pay.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Russians took part in protest marches and strikes on Thursday, waving red banners and demanding back wages, as a nationwide day of action got under way in the Far East.
The numbers involved, however, suggested that the figure of 20 million protestors which trade unions had forecast across the country may have been optimistic.

In Vladivostok, Russia's main Pacific port, thousands marched demanding payment of billions of dollars in overdue pay and pensions. Some called for President Boris Yeltsin and his newly appointed government to resign.
Unions put the turnout at 50,000, the police at just 15,000.

Workers at some thousand companies in Vladivostok's Primorsk region were on strike, labour leaders said. But with much of its industry already at a virtual standstill and millions of workers without pay, the effects of such action appear very limited.

Police reported no incidents in Vladivostok, a city of some half a million, nor elsewhere across the sparsely populated far eastern regions. There was a considerable police presence in Vladivostok, combined with union stewards.
The mood of many of the marchers seemed generally more festive than angry, reminding observers of traditional Soviet era May Day parades of workers. Many carried red banners.

"First wages, then taxes," read one banner flying above a crowd of about one thousand in the centre of the far eastern city of Magadan, once the clearing centre for some of the worst gulag labour camps. The government, reshuffled this week, has made a priority of collecting taxes in order to pay its bills.
Some local politicians have thrown their voices behind the protests, as has the communist-dominated national parliament.
In Moscow, there was little obvious strike action early in the morning. Public transport was running normally. Marches were due to start in the city centre in the afternoon.

Dozens of armed OMON police commandos in riot gear already lined a street south of the centre where protesters were due to gather. Several police trucks were parked close to the White House government building. But otherwise there was little sign of a heavy police presence on a cold but sunny Moscow morning.
In President Boris Yeltsin's home district near the Urals city of Yekaterinburg, unions said pickets were blocking the main highway to Siberia.
